I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette:
Yousef was a 30-year-old divorced tax inspector who had come to treatment after months of feeling as though his life had narrowed to the distance between his apartment, his desk at work, and the phone in his hand. The collision that changed things had happened on an evening drive home after work, when a car coming through an intersection struck his vehicle hard enough to spin it sideways and leave him trapped amid the smell of fuel, shattered glass, and a sharp alcohol odor from the other driver. He had survived with injuries that healed, but the experience stayed in him as a series of vivid fragments: the crumpled cars, the jolt of impact, the sound of metal, and the sense that ordinary driving had become a place where death could arrive without warning. Even now, if he saw cars hit by accident in a news clip or passed a similar model on the road, the scene would jump back with such force that he felt pulled straight into it again. The smell of alcohol could do the same, collapsing the present into that night, and for a moment he would feel as if danger were right beside him. Those moments left him immediately on guard, scanning for what might come next, and his body reacted before his mind could catch up; an unexpected horn, a door slam, even a dropped stack of files in the office could make him startle in a way that embarrassed him and then kept him watchful for the rest of the day.

After the crash, Yousef began to tell himself that he could not rely on himself anymore. He had once seen himself as disciplined, practical, and competent - the sort of man who handled numbers, deadlines, and responsibility without hesitation - but now he felt no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. He noticed that he was driving more tensely, second-guessing himself at every turn, and each time he felt shaken he took it as proof that something in him had broken. He was also certain that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again; if he felt fear, he read it as weakness, and if he felt flat or distant, he read that too as damage. Those beliefs pushed him away from situations that might stir them up. He stopped driving except when absolutely necessary and refused to be a passenger in other people's cars, even declining offers from relatives who wanted to help. He began organizing his days around avoiding roads, traffic, and the possibility of being trapped in a vehicle, and that avoidance spread into smaller habits too: he would spend long hours on his phone, games, or the internet to keep his mind occupied, and he often restricted food because appetite felt like another body signal he could not trust. The more he withdrew, the more he noticed how little control he seemed to have, and that fed the belief that he was not the man he had been.

At work, the consequences became harder to hide. As a tax inspector, Yousef used to spend long hours visiting businesses, riding between sites, and moving confidently through the city; now he arranged routes to avoid busy roads and felt his chest tighten whenever a similar car appeared beside him in traffic. The office itself was not free of reminders: a report about a collision, a colleague mentioning a drinking weekend, or the sudden honk of a delivery truck outside could send his attention snapping outward, searching for threat. Because he was always scanning, he found it harder to concentrate on case files, and because he had been spending so much time online to escape his thoughts, he arrived tired and irritable, which only confirmed to him that he was failing. He started to feel that his routines were proving his own inadequacy. What frightened him most was that each time he withdrew into the phone, skipped meals, or avoided the road, he came away feeling even less capable and even more on edge, and that heightened state made the world seem full of cues that could drag him back into the crash. A similar car on the street, the odor of alcohol at a family gathering, or the sudden bang of a closing door could set off the same chain again, and he would tense, scan, and recoil, then escape further into distraction and restriction to get through the day. By the time he sought help, Yousef was exhausted by the cycle and ashamed of how much his life had shrunk. He said he wanted to drive his own life again, but he was most afraid that the crash had permanently taken away the man he used to be.
